tagline.text: A hike that looks down on a winding river, then wades into a river of white rock

location.label: Location
location.text: Daraitan, Tanay, Rizal (on the boundary with General Nakar, Quezon)

children.text: Climb a limestone peak about 739m above sea level at the southern tip of the Sierra Madre to look down on a winding river and mountain ridges, then swim and explore caves at the Tinipak River, where jade-colored water flows between white marble boulders — Manila's most popular day hike.
Mount Daraitan is a limestone peak about

above sea level, rising on the boundary between Daraitan village in Tanay, Rizal, and General Nakar, Quezon. Sitting at the southern tip of the Sierra Madre, the Philippines' longest mountain range, the summit offers a sweeping view of endless green ridges and the Tinipak River (the upper course of the Agos River), which snakes between them like a serpent. On clear mornings you can also see a sea of clouds filling the valley.

What makes this mountain special is that you can enjoy both hiking and swimming in a single day. Descending the far side of the summit brings you to the Tinipak River, where huge white marble and limestone boulders lie scattered along the water and jade-colored currents flow between them. Along the riverbank is also Tinipak Cave, holding pools of cold spring water — cooling off in the river and cave after a sweaty climb is the classic way to do the Daraitan hike.

The Daraitan area is also home to the indigenous Dumagat-Remontado people. To them the Tinipak River is considered sacred, and villagers run the tourism trade through guiding, tricycle service, and small restaurants. Registration and guide assignment are managed by the barangay (village) tourism office, so the system is fairly well organized.

The climb is steep with rocky sections, but the trail is short enough that beginners can manage it with reasonable fitness. It's especially recommended for those wanting a real sense of achievement on a first hike, groups of friends who want to swim after hiking, and anyone chasing photogenic scenery.

blocks.title: The winding river seen from the summit

children.text: It usually takes about
2–3 hours
from the registration point to the summit. From the viewpoint at the edge of the rocks, the Tinipak River unfolds below in a great curve through the ridges.
The spot near the summit with a heart-shaped structure framing the river bend behind it is Daraitan's signature photo location. It's popular enough that you may have to wait your turn on weekends.
On dry-season mornings, the valley often fills completely with cloud. If you want to see the sea of clouds, you'll need to register around
3–4 AM
and set off in the dark.
Swim and take photos in the shallow pools between the white boulders. With sunlight glinting off the rock and the water so clear, the whole river feels like one giant natural swimming pool.

blocks.title: Tinipak Cave and its spring-fed pool

children.text: Enter the cave among the riverside rocks and squeeze through a narrow gap to reach a very cold underground pool. You follow a guide with a headlamp on a short exploration, and the cave entrance fee is paid separately.

blocks.title: Crossing the river by raft or bridge

children.text: Reaching the village means crossing the Tanay River. When the bridge is usable, you cross straight over by tricycle, but when high water puts the bridge out of use, riding a bamboo raft (balsa) is an experience unique to this place.

If you come for two days and one night, you can spend the night under the stars at a designated campsite along the Tinipak River. Having the river almost entirely to yourself the next morning is camping's biggest reward here.

During the wet season,
June–October

, the trail turns slippery and leeches appear, and above all the Tinipak River becomes dangerous. Rain in the mountains upstream can turn the river into brown floodwater within minutes even while the village stays dry. During typhoon warnings or heavy rain, the village closes off hiking and river access, so be sure to check the Daraitan tourism office's latest notices before you set out. Hikers crowd in heavily on weekends and holidays, so choosing a weekday is a good idea if you can.

Most visitors go for the day, but for an easier pre-dawn registration, you can stay the night before at a homestay or simple lodging in Daraitan village, or at accommodation in Tanay town. Village homestays are basic, at about

per person, and many people also pitch a tent at the designated campsite along the Tinipak River. If you'd rather have more comfort, use the resorts and campgrounds around Marcos Highway in upland Tanay (about
per night).
The village has several small eateries (carinderias) catering to hikers, serving Filipino home cooking like adobo, sinigang, and fried fish for about

a meal. A glass of buko (young coconut) juice or a halo-halo after the descent tastes wonderful. There are almost no restaurants by the river itself, so bring a packed lunch or snacks, or ask your guide to have lunch packed from the village. Grabbing a late lunch in Tanay town on the way back is also a good option.
Registration is only taken on-site, and some days have a cap on the number of hikers. Slots can fill up before sunrise on weekends, so try to arrive as early as possible.
The barangay hall registration desk opens at
3 AM
, and the number of daily hikers is limited to about 300. There is no online booking or electronic payment, so on weekends and holidays arrive before the desk opens.
Bring ID, and pay the environmental fee and guide fee in cash. There's no ATM in the village, so bring cash from Tanay or Manila.
The rocks near the summit are sharp limestone. Gloves and hiking shoes with good grip make things much safer.
The descent is steeper and longer than the climb and puts real strain on the knees. Trekking poles are worth bringing.
Bring at least 2 liters of water per person, a headlamp, a dry bag, a change of clothes, and aqua shoes. The riverside rocks are slippery and can get hot.
Inside Tinipak Cave you'll get wet and it's very cold. Put your phone in a dry bag and stay with your guide.
Carry out all your trash. Since the river is sacred to the indigenous community, don't use soap or shampoo in the water.
Combining this with Masungi Georeserve or Daranak Falls on the same day is tight, so if you're making a Rizal province trip of it, plan for one overnight stay.

Even on a clear day, the Tinipak River can rise suddenly from rain upstream — if the water turns cloudy or the current picks up, get out of the river immediately. The nearby Kaliwa Dam, being built to supply drinking water to Metro Manila, also means river sections and access rules may change as construction and impoundment progress. Check the Daraitan tourism office's latest notices before you set out.
In the river, swim only in the shallow areas your guide allows, and don't dive off the rocks. Some spots are deeper and swifter than they look.
The summit viewpoint rocks sit right at the cliff edge. Don't stand at the unguarded edge while taking photos.
In the wet season, leeches appear on the trail and the rocks get very slippery. It's safer to postpone the hike if it's raining.
Climbing without a guide or venturing off the designated trail is prohibited.
Midday sun reflecting off the white riverside rocks is very strong, causing frequent sunburn and dehydration. Bring sunscreen and a hat.
